articles.title: Re: Assisted dying bill rejected: how doctors helped shape the debate
articles.description: Agreement: I Agree Body: Dear Editor, Re: Assisted dying bill rejected: how doctors helped shape the debate by Adrian O’Dowd BMJ 2026;394:e100854 http://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2026-100854 Published: 14 September 2026 I read with interest O’Dowd’s recent news review of the rejection of the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill. As an NHS nurse working in ITU who has had a personal family experience of assisted dying, I am both personally and professionally devastated that legislation has not been passed. My devastation is compounded by the fact that MPs had previously demonstrated majority support for this legislation, with polling demonstrating overwhelming majority public support as well – support MPs were unable to coalesce. This has been, and will be remembered as, a failure of parliamentary process and a failure of government to do the right thing. Though palliative medicine is brilliant, in our work we routinely see patients suffering at the end of life despite exemplary palliative care. It is misleading to argue that palliative care is a panacea. There have been missed opportunities by the BMA and others to challenge such significant misleading arguments by practicing physicians during these debates. Conservative MP Rebecca Smith quoted palliative care consultants in her constituency who said they were ‘not prepared to take part in assisted dying’, remarking that they would ‘leave the profession’ over the issue. This is hyperbole at best and patient abandonment at worst. It was clear in this legislation (and in legislation across the globe) that clinicians are not mandated to participate in assisted dying, with conscientious objectors consistently respected. Smith asks ‘How can we offer palliative care at the same time as assisted dying?’ – I will tell you how, through the personal experience of my Mum, who resided in Canada prior to her death. Diagnosed with metastatic melanoma, she received palliative radiotherapy and met with various oncologists and palliative care consultants who deemed she was not fit for immunotherapy nor any other therapies. She chose to have an assisted death at home, having been assessed for it by both hospital and community doctors who were entirely separate from her palliative care team. In the end, her death was facilitated by a GP, not by anyone involved in her palliative care, though as a family we would have been more than happy either way. Whether or not her palliative care team were personally supportive of her decision or were conscientious objectors was never elucidated to us, and was entirely irrelevant. In your article Labour MP Zubir Ahmed expressed concerns about assisted dying with respect to defining terminal illness, mentioning predicting individual patient responses to immunotherapy as a concrete example of where this can be difficult. Though I would concede this point, I would argue the answer to this isn’t to then block choice from those facing death, but to instead widen the criteria to those with unendurable suffering as defined by the patient. Prognostication of less than six months to live is entirely arbitrary and unnecessary - and in my Mum’s case, had she been a candidate for immunotherapy, I’m confident she would have initiated that treatment whilst simultaneously exploring her other options, one of which was assisted dying. In a misguided attempt to ‘protect’ patients and ensure equity, MPs have failed to pass safe legislation and have chosen to continue a true inequity, whereby wealthy UK residents can travel to Europe to seek an assisted death, and those without the means to do so are left adrift. I am so grateful my Mum emigrated to Canada and had the choice as she faced death, and I only wish the same could be true for all of us residents in the UK today. Sincerely, Luke Costello, RN Board Member of My Death, My Decision No competing Interests: No competing interests The following competing Interests: Board member of My Death, My Decision.
